content: The collaboration with the pharmaceutical industry was organized through the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association and the Developing Country Vaccine Manufacturer Network. The final recommendations, including GRADE assessments, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and other relevant components, were incorporated into the WHO Guidelines for Malaria and submitted for review by the Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) alongside the development of the WHO position paper published in the Weekly Epidemiologic Record. The glossary includes terms from the updated 2021 WHO malaria terminology, which were reviewed and agreed upon by the Drafting Committee on Malaria Terminology, first convened in 2015. For further details on the committee and the process of reviewing and updating malaria terminology, as well as additional notes on the glossary, please refer to the relevant document. Adherence: Refers to compliance with a prescribed regimen (e.g., chemoprophylaxis or treatment) or adherence to procedures and practices recommended by a healthcare provider. Adverse drug reaction: A harmful and unintended response to a medication occurring at doses typically used in humans. Adverse event: Any unexpected medical occurrence in a person exposed to a biological or chemical product, which may not necessarily have a causal relationship with the product. Serious adverse event: A medical occurrence in a person exposed to a product that results in death, requires or prolongs hospitalization, causes significant disability or incapacity, or is life-threatening. Aestivation: A survival process in mosquitoes involving behavioral and physiological changes during periods of drought or high temperatures. Age group: A subgroup of a population classified by age, typically divided into categories such as 0–11 months, 12–23 months, 2–4 years, 5–9 years, 10–14 years, 15–19 years, and ≥20 years. Physiological age (mosquitoes): Refers to the number of gonotrophic cycles completed by an adult female mosquito, categorized as nulliparous, primiparous, 2-parous, 3-parous, etc. Case (fever): The occurrence of fever (current or recent) in an individual. Imported case: A malaria case or infection acquired outside the area where it is diagnosed. Index case: A case whose epidemiological characteristics trigger additional active case or infection detection. It may also refer to the case identified as the origin of infection for one or more introduced cases. Indigenous case: A case contracted locally with no evidence of importation or direct link to transmission from an imported case. Induced case: A case originating from blood transfusion or other parenteral inoculation of the parasite, rather than natural mosquito-borne transmission. Introduced case: A locally contracted case with strong epidemiological evidence linking it directly to a known imported case (first-generation local transmission). Locally acquired case: A case acquired locally through mosquito-borne transmission. Malaria case: The occurrence of malaria infection in a person confirmed by the presence of malaria parasites in the blood through diagnostic testing. Presumed case: A suspected malaria case not confirmed by diagnostic testing. Recrudescent case: A malaria case attributed to the recurrence of asexual parasitemia after antimalarial treatment due to incomplete clearance of the same genotype(s) that caused the original illness. This must be distinguished from reinfection and relapse (in the case of P. vivax and P. ovale). Relapsing case: A malaria case caused by the activation of dormant liver-stage hypnozoites of P. vivax or P. ovale acquired previously. Suspected malaria case: An illness suspected by a healthcare worker to be due to malaria, typically based on the presence of fever with or without other symptoms. Case detection: A surveillance activity involving the search for malaria cases in a community. Active case detection: The detection of malaria cases by healthcare workers at the community or household level, often in high-risk population groups. Case management: The process of diagnosing, treating, providing clinical care, counseling, and following up on symptomatic malaria infections. Case notification: The mandatory reporting of all malaria cases by medical units and practitioners to the health department or malaria control program, as required by national laws or regulations. Catchment area: A defined geographical area served by a health program or institution, such as a hospital or community health center, delineated based on population distribution, natural boundaries, and transport accessibility. Cerebral malaria: Severe P. falciparum malaria characterized by impaired consciousness (Glasgow coma scale <11 or Blantyre coma scale <3) persisting for more than one hour after a seizure. Certification of malaria-free status: Certification granted by WHO after proving beyond reasonable doubt that local human malaria transmission by Anopheles mosquitoes has been interrupted in an entire country for at least three consecutive years, with a national surveillance system and prevention program in place. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention: The intermittent administration of full treatment courses of an antimalarial medicine during the malaria season to prevent illness, maintaining therapeutic drug concentrations in the blood during periods of highest malaria risk. Chemoprophylaxis: The administration of a medicine at predefined intervals to prevent the development or progression of an infection into manifest disease. Cluster: An aggregation of relatively uncommon events or diseases in space and/or time in numbers greater than expected by chance. Combination therapy: The use of two or more classes of antimalarial medicines with unrelated mechanisms of action. Coverage: The proportion of a population in a specific area receiving a particular intervention. Optimal coverage: The result of a prioritization process guiding resource allocation decisions, combining impact analysis, value for money, and stakeholder engagement while considering equity implications. Universal health coverage: Ensuring all individuals and communities receive the health services they need without financial hardship, encompassing health promotion, prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care. Cure: The elimination of all malaria parasites causing the infection from an infected person. Radical cure: The elimination of both blood-stage and latent liver infection in cases of P. vivax and P. ovale, thereby preventing relapses. Cure rate: The percentage of treated individuals whose infection is cured. Cyto-adherence: The tendency of malaria-infected erythrocytes to adhere to the endothelium of the host's internal organ microvasculature. Diagnosis: The process of determining the cause of an illness, including clinical assessment and diagnostic testing. Molecular diagnosis: The use of nucleic acid amplification-based tests to detect malaria parasites. Parasitological diagnosis: The detection of malaria parasites, Plasmodium-specific antigens, or genes in the blood of an infected individual. Diapause: A condition of suspended animation or temporary arrest in the development of immature and adult mosquitoes. Dosage regimen: The prescribed formulation, route of administration, dose, dosing interval, and duration of treatment with a medicine. Loading dose: An initial dose or series of doses given at the start of therapy to rapidly achieve the target concentration. Drug efficacy: The ability of an antimalarial medicine to achieve the therapeutic objective when administered at a recommended dose, with minimal toxicity. Drug resistance: The ability of a parasite strain to survive and/or multiply despite the absorption of a medicine given in doses equal to or higher than those usually recommended. Drug safety: The characteristics of a medicine reflecting its potential to cause harm, including identified and potential risks. Gametocytocidal drug: A drug that kills male and/or female gametocytes, preventing them from infecting mosquitoes. Schizontocidal drug: A drug that kills schizonts in the liver or blood. Endemic area: An area with ongoing, measurable malaria transmission over successive years. Endemicity level: The degree of malaria transmission in an area. Endophagy: The tendency of mosquitoes to blood-feed indoors. Endophily: The tendency of mosquitoes to rest indoors. Entomological inoculation rate (EIR): The number of infectious bites received per person in a given unit of time in a human population. Epidemic: The occurrence of malaria cases significantly exceeding the expected number in a given place and time. Epidemiological investigation: The study of environmental, human, and entomological factors determining the incidence or prevalence of infection or disease. Erythrocytic cycle: The portion of the malaria parasite's life cycle from merozoite invasion of red blood cells to schizont rupture. Exophagy: The tendency of mosquitoes to feed outdoors. Exophily: The tendency of mosquitoes to rest outdoors. Experimental huts: Simulated houses with entry and exit traps for sampling mosquitoes entering and exiting, blood-feeding indoors, and surviving or dying in each sub-sample. Fixed-dose combination: A formulation combining two antimalarial medicines in the same tablet, capsule, powder, suspension, or granule. Malaria focus: A defined area containing the epidemiological and ecological factors necessary for malaria transmission. Gametocyte: The sexual stage of malaria parasites that can infect Anopheles mosquitoes when ingested during a blood meal. Gametocyte rate: The percentage of individuals in a defined population with detectable sexual forms of malaria parasites. Geographical reconnaissance: Census and mapping to determine the distribution of the human population and other features relevant to malaria transmission, guiding interventions. Gonotrophic cycle (mosquito): The period of reproductive development in female mosquitoes, including host-seeking, blood-feeding, digestion, ovarian development, searching for a breeding site, and oviposition. Gonotrophic discordance: Female mosquitoes taking more than one blood meal per gonotrophic cycle. Hibernation: A process in which mosquitoes survive cold periods through behavioral or physiological changes. House: Any structure other than a tent or mobile shelter where humans sleep. Household: The ecosystem, including people and animals occupying the same house and the accompanying vectors. House-spraying: The application of liquid insecticide formulations to specified (mostly interior) surfaces of buildings. Human landing catch: A method for collecting vectors as they land on individuals. Hyperparasitemia: A high density of parasites in the blood, increasing the risk of severe malaria. Hypnozoite: The dormant liver stage of P. vivax and P. ovale malaria that remains in host hepatocytes for variable periods before activation and development into a pre-erythrocytic schizont, causing a blood-stage infection (relapse). Importation rate: The rate of parasite influx via infected individuals or infected Anopheles mosquitoes. Infectivity: The ability of Plasmodium sporozoites to infect humans or mosquitoes. Insecticide: A chemical product (natural or synthetic) that kills insects. Residual insecticides: Insecticides that remain active for an extended period after application. Integrated vector management (IVM): Rational decision-making for optimal use of resources for vector control. Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp): A full therapeutic course of antimalarial medicine given to pregnant women at routine prenatal visits, regardless of infection status. Larval source management: Management of aquatic habitats to prevent the development of immature mosquito stages. Long-lasting insecticidal net (LLIN): A factory-treated mosquito net with insecticide incorporated into or bound around the fibers, retaining effective biological activity for at least 20 WHO standard washes and three years of recommended use. Malaria elimination: Malaria eradication: The permanent reduction to zero of worldwide malaria incidence caused by human malaria parasites, with no further interventions required. Malaria infection: The presence of Plasmodium parasites in blood or tissues, confirmed by diagnostic testing. Malaria mortality rate: The number of deaths from malaria per unit of population during a defined period. Malaria pigment (haemozoin): A granular material formed by malaria parasites as a by-product of hemoglobin digestion. Malaria prevalence: The proportion of a specified population with malaria infection at one time. Malaria rebound: Increased malaria incidence following a time-limited reduction in transmission due to interventions. Malaria receptivity: The degree to which an ecosystem allows for malaria transmission. Malaria reintroduction: The occurrence of introduced cases in a previously malaria-free area. Malaria risk stratification: Classification of geographical areas based on factors determining receptivity and vulnerability to malaria transmission. Mass drug administration (MDA): The administration of a full treatment course of an antimalarial to all age groups in a defined area at the same time, often at repeated intervals. Mass screening: Population-wide assessment of malaria risk factors to identify subgroups for further intervention. Mass testing and treatment: Parasitological screening of an entire population in a defined area, treating those with a positive test result. Medicine safety: Characteristics of a medicine reflecting its potential to cause harm. Merozoite: The extracellular stage of a parasite released into host plasma when a schizont ruptures. Moderate to high perennial transmission: Persistent P. falciparum transmission resulting in parasite prevalence >10% or annual parasite incidence >250 per 1000. Monotherapy: Antimalarial treatment with a single active compound or a synergistic combination of two compounds with related mechanisms of action. National focus register: A centralized database of all malaria foci in a country. National malaria case register: A centralized database with individual records of all malaria cases in a country. Insecticide-treated net (ITN): A mosquito net treated with insecticide to repel, disable, or kill mosquitoes. Oocyst: A stage of the malaria parasite developing from the ookinete on the outer wall of the mosquito midgut. Parasitemia: The presence of parasites in the blood. Parasite clearance time: The time between the first drug administration and the first examination showing no parasites in the blood. Parasite density: The number of asexual parasites per unit volume of blood. Patent period: The period during which malaria parasitemia is detectable. Plasmodium: A genus of protozoan blood parasites causing malaria. This comprehensive glossary provides detailed definitions and explanations of terms related to malaria, its transmission, diagnosis, treatment, and control.
